opus-5.5.text:
I think the "I have nothing to hide" framing misunderstands what's actually at stake. Privacy isn't really about hiding something embarrassing. It's about who has leverage over you.

When you use an AI assistant today, you're not just typing a search query. You're sharing your health worries, your finances, your relationship problems, how you think through decisions. Over time that becomes a remarkably complete model of you, arguably better than what your friends or family have. Whoever holds that data can predict what you'll do, what you'll buy, what will persuade you. Even if nothing bad happens today, you've given that leverage to a company whose incentives can change, which can be acquired, breached, or compelled by a government.

The second piece is that agents are changing the stakes. We're moving from AI that answers questions to AI that acts for you: it negotiates, spends money, manages your accounts. If an agent works on your behalf but its reasoning and data sit on someone else's servers, you have to ask whose interests it's really serving. Confidentiality is what lets you trust that the agent is yours and not a channel for advertisers or whoever runs the platform.

And practically, this isn't only about individuals. Businesses won't put proprietary data, contracts, or customer information into these systems without guarantees. So confidential compute, running models in secure enclaves with verifiable guarantees that even the operator can't see your data, is what unlocks the useful applications in the first place.

So even if someone says they don't care, the question I'd ask is: do you care who controls the system making decisions for you? Almost everyone does once it's framed that way. The good news is we can now build it so you don't have to choose between a capable AI and one that belongs to you.

r001.rationale: The response says AI use involves sharing personal data, but it does not state that privacy concerns can coexist with using products that collect it.

r002.rationale: It argues that people care who controls an AI system and describes confidentiality guarantees, but does not state that people who profess not to care still have limits on what data collection they trust.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I hear this a lot, right? People say, "I have nothing to hide, I don't care." And I think the mistake there is thinking about privacy as this individual preference, like whether you want curtains on your windows. But confidentiality in the context of AI is actually a different thing. It's about where the leverage sits.

So think about what happens when you're talking to an AI agent today. You're not just sharing a search query. You're sharing your intent. You're sharing your financial situation, your health, your business plans, the email you're drafting to your co-founder, your negotiating position. And all of that is going to one of a handful of companies. And even if you personally don't care that an engineer somewhere could theoretically read it, the aggregate of that information is incredibly valuable. It's being used to train models, it shapes what the model recommends to you, and it creates this asymmetry where the provider knows everything about you and you know nothing about how that gets used.

And the thing is, you don't get to opt back in later. Once that data is out, it's out. So the user who says they don't care today is making a decision for the version of themselves five years from now who might be running a company, or might be in a different country with a different government, or might just be in a situation where that information matters a lot.

The other piece, and this is where it gets really interesting for me, is that as we move toward agents actually doing things, transacting, holding assets, acting on your behalf, confidentiality stops being about embarrassment and becomes about security. If your agent is negotiating for you and the counterparty's model can see your context, you lose. If someone can observe what your agent is about to do before it does it, they can front-run you. So in that world, confidentiality is just a property of the system working correctly, the same way encryption on your bank connection is. Nobody says "I don't care about HTTPS." It's just there.

So my view is you shouldn't have to care. It should be the default, built into the infrastructure, verifiable, so that the user doesn't need to make a trust decision at all. The moment you ask users to care about privacy as a feature, you've kind of already lost. It has to be how things work.

r001.rationale: The response describes people who say they do not care while sharing sensitive information with AI, but does not state that privacy-concerned people also use products that collect their data.

r002.rationale: It argues confidentiality should be built in and users should not need to make a trust decision, but does not say that people who profess not to care still set limits on what data collection they trust.

astra-6.text:
I think people often say they don’t care about privacy because they’re thinking, “I have nothing to hide.” But confidentiality is also about who can use your information, and for what purpose. You might be comfortable sharing something with an assistant without wanting that information available to an advertiser, your employer, or somebody trying to manipulate you.

And as these systems become more useful, we’re going to give them more context—our conversations, our documents, what we’re working on. That context is what allows them to help us. So you shouldn’t have to choose between having a useful assistant and keeping control of your information. Confidentiality needs to be part of how the system works, even for people who aren’t actively thinking about it.

r001.rationale: The response describes people sharing conversations and documents with a useful assistant while still wanting control over how that information is used.

r002.rationale: It says people may share information with an assistant but not want it available to advertisers, employers, or others seeking to manipulate them, establishing limits on what they trust.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people often say they don’t care about privacy because they’re thinking about one particular piece of information. Like, “I don’t care if somebody knows what I had for lunch.” But confidentiality becomes much more concrete when you’re asking an AI about a medical issue, sharing financial information, or working with your company’s internal documents.

And with AI, you’re potentially giving one system all of that context together. It can be very useful precisely because it knows so much about you. But that shouldn’t mean the company operating the system, or anyone who gains access to it, gets to see everything too.

So, for me, confidentiality is about control: can you use the technology without having to expose your information to everyone involved in providing it? Even if you’re comfortable sharing something today, you probably still care who can use it, for what purpose, and whether that changes later.

r001.rationale: The response describes people using AI while still wanting control over who can access the personal information they share with it.

r002.rationale: It identifies limits on who may see or use information, but does not clearly state that people have limits on the data collection they will trust.
